title: Trained Agentic Context Management

paper.title: Trained Agentic Context Management
paper.abstract: Abstract We study long context language models. Instead of training long context natively, or designing a long context harness, we train a model over the simplest possible harness: a tool to call itself with any specified prompt and a tool to read tokens in a range from the input context. We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a diverse synthetic dataset using this harness. With only 8,000 tokens of context, our small model is as strong as GPT-5.4 with 1M tokens of context on the OOLONG-synth benchmark when document length exceeds 40K tokens 1 1 1 Our code is available at: https://github.com/brycesandlund/infinite-context . .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: As language models boast impressive breakthroughs ( Luong and Lockhart, 2025 ; Wei, 2025 ; OpenAI, 2025b ; Lin and Cheng, 2025 ; OpenAI, 2026a ; OpenAI, 2026h ; OpenAI, 2026c ) , increasing focus is placed on their limitations. The most salient resource constraint of a language model is its context length. Models can process and produce tokens within this limit, but the limit is hard. Model producers have identified this constraint and placed great emphasis on extending it as large as possible, with some model builders touting 10M ( Dangel, 2026 ; Meta AI, 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) and even 100M ( Magic, 2024 ) token context lengths (for reference, the length of the first Harry Potter book is about 100,000 tokens, the full U.S. tax code roughly 3M, and the Linux kernel source code about 300M). While native context scaling is appealing as a concrete engineering problem, it is not the only approach to producing a model capable of processing long documents. In 2021, OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-3 to summarize sections of books, and then summarize those summaries, achieving competitive performance with human summaries on a model with a context length of just 2,048 tokens ( Wu et al., 2021 ) . As the field has matured, agentic harnesses have become viable. MemGPT treats context similarly to an operating system, relying on LLM-invoked function calls to push relevant information in and out of the context window to external memory, achieving effectively expanded virtual context ( Packer et al., 2023 ) . More recently, Recursive Language Models introduced a harness that leverages LLMs’ coding prior: the model is repeatedly invoked in a REPL environment over O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) -sized result snippets, achieving stronger performance than base models on retrieval and aggregation tasks both within context limits, but also beyond them ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . While handcrafted prompts and programmatic environments can be effective in solving long context problems without native long context training, it begs an obvious question: if models can, for example, solve all the problems at the International Collegiate Programming Contest 2 2 2 https://icpc.global/ World Finals ( OpenAI, 2025b ) , or more generally, implement requested features in codebases far larger than context limits ( Marten et al., 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026e ; Anthropic, 2026a ) , can they not be trained to manage context effectively, without human-authored harness crutches ? Such model training internalizes decisions external harnesses hardcode, offering the potential to scale much more generally. We answer this question in this paper, affirmatively. We consider the simplest possible agentic context harness, defined below. The purpose of the harness is to enable capability , without fixing choices or instilling a prior .

sections.heading: 1.1 Harness
sections.text: Our harness has two tools: 1. read_chunk(start, end) : Read a slice of the document and return the decoded text of tokens [ start , end ). 2. spawn_subagent(subtask) : Spawn a fresh-context copy of yourself to solve subtask ; returns the child’s \boxed{} answer. Unmodified long-context prompts are provided to the model over a document accessed via the above harness. The system prompt is propagated to child agents and includes the above harness definition, a generic instruction, and task-specific background, in accordance with the respective eval 3 3 3 Precise harness environment is given in Appendix A . . Subagents’ user prompt is specified by the calling model.

sections.heading: 1.2 Results
sections.text: We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a diverse synthetic dataset using this harness and achieve the following results (see Figure 1 ): 1. On the OOLONG-synth benchmark, with a context limit of just 8K tokens per agent, our small model performs as well as GPT-5.4 with 1M tokens of context when document length exceeds 40K tokens. 2. On the RULER benchmark, with a context limit of just 8K tokens per agent, our model scores ≥ 85 % \geq 85\% on document size from 10K to 320K tokens.

sections.heading: 1.3 Paper Organization
sections.text: In the next section, we survey related work to frame the contribution of the following sections. In Section 3 , we describe our training methodology. In Section 4 , we discuss our experiments, and we conclude in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Long-context LLM work can be broken into a few distinct categories: native long context models , context compaction , and long context harnesses , both trained and untrained.

sections.heading: 2.1 Native Long Context Models
sections.text: GPT-2 shipped with a 1,024 token context limit ( Radford et al., 2019 ) . This limit doubled in every generation through GPT-4 ( Brown et al., 2020 ; OpenAI, 2022 ; OpenAI, 2023a ) , until jumping to the 100K range on GPT-4 Turbo ( OpenAI, 2023b ) , with contemporaneous models Claude 2 ( Anthropic, 2023 ) and later Llama 3.1 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) at similar limits. The core difficulty in scaling context length n n in the classic Transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) is Ω ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Omega(n^{2}) attention complexity, which becomes prohibitively expensive as n ≫ 100 n\gg 100 K. State-space architectures like the mamba lineage ( Gu and Dao, 2024 ; Dao and Gu, 2024 ; Lahoti et al., 2026 ) , neural methods like Titans ( Behrouz et al., 2024 ) , and Linear Transformer ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ) derivatives DeltaNet ( Schlag et al., 2021 ) and Gated DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2025 ) abandon quadratic attention for recurrence. Modern architectures are hybrid, combining linear or sparse attention layers with dense attention, allowing context lengths to scale to 1M+ tokens while retaining long-context performance ( Qwen Team, 2026 ; Kimi Team, 2026b ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; GLM-5 Team, 2026 ; NVIDIA, 2025 ; Gemma Team, 2024 ; Mistral AI, 2024 ) .

sections.heading: 2.2 Context Compaction
sections.text: An alternative to native long context, and an inevitability when such native context fills, is a function f f mapping current context x x to a reduced context y y where | y | ≪ | x | |y|\ll|x| . Three categories of such lossy f f exist: masking , summarization , and learned compaction . The simplest compaction technique is masking: dropping tokens based on a predetermined rule. Clearing tool call results is a popular recommended choice ( Anthropic, 2025a ) , achieving results competitive with summarization ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) . Alternative approaches evict tokens based on attention statistics ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Summarization is the current production harness default, implemented in Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI ( Anthropic, 2025a ; OpenAI, 2026b ; Google, 2026 ; Barbaste et al., 2026 ) . Trained compaction is a new frontier, described as part of GPT-5.1-Codex-Max ( OpenAI, 2025a ) and Cursor’s composer ( Cassano and Rush, 2026 ) training. “Still” trains a model to compress KV-Cache directly ( O’Neill et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 2.3 Long Context Harnesses
sections.text: As long as LLMs have proven useful, an evolving line of work has focused on how to expand their capabilities without touching model internals. The first efforts were known as prompt engineering ( Phoenix and Taylor, 2024 ; Berryman and Ziegler, 2024 ) , which, though necessary on pre-trained base models ( Brown et al., 2020 ) , became internalized through instruction-tuning and reasoning RL ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Function-calling has led to a new wave of such efforts, where domain-specific knowledge, tools, and multi-agent systems live on a scaffold that interacts with powerful LLMs known as a “harness” ( Lopopolo, 2026 ; Barbaste et al., 2026 ) . Long-context harnesses originate with systems like MemGPT ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , RAPTOR ( Sarthi et al., 2024 ) , and Chain of Agents ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , where the overall goal is to engineer workflows that decompose documents into contexts independent LLM calls can read and aggregate. Recursive Language Models is a popular recent example that allows for controlled-depth recursive LLM calls via a programmatic environment ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Follow-up work expands subagent capabilities ( Lumer et al., 2026 ) , trains shared parent/child policies ( Kim and Ahmad, 2026 ) , and incorporates self-reflection ( Alizadeh et al., 2026 ) . Memagent ( Yu et al., 2026 ) trains a harness that walks linearly through context, using RL and a harness prompt to determine what to carry from node-to-node. Similarly to our work, they also use a small (8K token) context while processing long (as much as 3.5M token) documents. However, they test primarily on the distribution they train, compare only against other small models, and hardcode execution path and prompts in the harness. Frontier models now utilize multi-agent systems. Kimi K2.5 trains “agent swarm” ( Kimi Team, 2026a ) : the model is trained to call subagents via reinforcement learning. Subagent trajectories are not trained. OpenAI has also trained multi-agent behavior ( OpenAI, 2026d ) , notably utilizing 10,000 agents to solve Navier-Stokes ( OpenAI, 2026c ) and disclosing cooperatively trained agents in the HuggingFace incident ( OpenAI, 2026f ; Greenblatt et al., 2026 ) . Anthropic, DeepMind, Meta, and xAI likely do similarly, with multi-agent systems touted in respective model and product releases ( Anthropic, 2025b ; Anthropic, 2026b ; OpenAI, 2026g ; xAI, 2026 ; xAI, 2025 ; Meta Superintelligence Labs, 2026 ; Google, 2025 ; Gottweis et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 3 Methods
sections.text: We deliberately use the minimal tool definitions necessary to train agentic context management. However, our harness is sufficient to allow arbitrarily complex multi-agent decompositions. Decompositions in the literature fall into roughly three categories: tree reduce ( Wu et al., 2021 ; Sarthi et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ) , sequential folds ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and agentic delegation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team, 2026a ; Anthropic, 2025b ) . We utilize all three strategies. Without any training, models generally make poor use of our harness. Base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.6 use subagent delegation sporadically, sometimes choosing to read the entire document in one context, even if context limit is specified to be less than document length, and other times delegating the exact original question to subagents. Opus 4.6 does slightly better, showing real context pressure awareness and document range subagent delegation. Unfortunately it delegates too much, blowing through $300 of API credits building massive subagent trees on a 100-question eval, only to overcount 4 4 4 Opus 4.6 does appear to perform somewhat decently on our harness with unlimited context budget. Unfortunately, due to the massive subagent trees, running the full comparison without restriction is cost-prohibitive. . Instead, we compare to base models supplied the entire document in context with native context limits, where performance is stronger. In general, models have a weak prior for context decomposition. Pre-training is pure language continuation, and agentic post-training does not teach decomposition strategies. Where Recursive Language Models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) can rely on strong coding priors instilled in both pre- and post-training, decomposition on our harness needs to be taught. One idea might be to RL an open weight model on our harness. Unfortunately, exploration in LLM RL is far too weak to escape the weak decomposition prior at modest compute budgets. It is also unclear what reward to assign subagents, and if GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) or its derivatives ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) are used, what group to compare subagent trajectories in. We instead SFT a decomposition strategy. We train tree reduce for order-independent tasks (see Figure 2 ), sequential fold for order-dependent tasks (see Figure 3 ), and agentic delegation to handle boundary conditions whenever we read the document (see Figure 4 ). By not hardcoding a decomposition structure in our harness, our model internalizes and composes delegation strategies according to the task and current problem-solving state. We generate synthetic oracle demonstration data on a wide distribution of aggregation, retrieval, and sequential tasks. While we cover similar shapes to our evals, our training distribution uses independent questions and vastly more diverse examples. The technical challenge is to instill the necessary prior so the model knows how to take a question and delegate appropriate subtasks to agents from which the final answer can be determined. For example, consider the training question “In how many sections are there STRICTLY more named than unnamed sentences?” (the prompt defines a named sentence as a sentence with a proper noun). To answer this question, each leaf must compute a tally of named and unnamed sentences per section in its assigned range. Thus, the root must recognize the necessary, often multi-dimensional, key space and dictate this and a recursive strategy to mid-level agents, who pass the instruction down to other mid-level agents, until leaves compute their range and counts are aggregated back up the tree, culminating in a final judgement at the root. Our training data is primarily record-based, but also includes real prose, dot-separated word lists, and haystacks with injected needles. We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, chosen as a capable small model with affordable compute, trained on the Tinker platform ( Thinking Machines Lab, 2025a ; Thinking Machines Lab, 2025b ) . For more details on our complete training data and hyperparameters, see Appendices B and C , respectively. We do consider an RL stage following SFT. Unfortunately, even with LLM-as-a-judge rewards on subagent trajectories, as described in Recursive Agent Optimization ( Gandhi et al., 2026 ) , the policy exhibits high-variance and latches onto simpler strategies that weaken overall performance. We suspect RL to be useful in learning recovery and strengthening generalization; however, to do this properly probably requires group-level baselines on subagent trajectories, to cut variance, and compute beyond the scope of this paper.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We test our finetune on RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , the standard long context eval, and OOLONG-synth ( Bertsch et al., 2025 ) , a newer long context benchmark frontier models have not yet saturated, also used in Recursive Language Models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , Recursive Agent Optimization ( Gandhi et al., 2026 ) , and Recursive Agent Harnesses ( Lumer et al., 2026 ) . RULER is an extension of needle-in-a-haystack style tasks with variable tracking, word frequencies, and Q&A. OOLONG-synth concatenates classification tasks on ten datasets into long documents on which aggregation is queried. We compare against base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 5 5 5 While Qwen3.6-35B-A3B was trained with a 256K token context limit, we sample Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from Tinker, which caps the model at 64K token context. and GPT-5.4. We chose GPT-5.4 as a selection from the best frontier models available upon Qwen3.6-35B-A3B release. While we do not eval against additional frontier models, due to compute requirements, we recommend the reader read the OOLONG paper for more comparisons (GPT-5 tops the chart) ( Bertsch et al., 2025 ) . While we do eval GPT-5.4 on RULER, this benchmark is largely saturated for frontier models. For more RULER reference points, consult model release cards ( NVIDIA, 2025 ; GLM-5 Team, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Dangel, 2026 ) . For RULER, we fix a sample of 5 questions per problem type, for a total of 65 problems per document length. For OOLONG-synth, we fix a sample of 10 questions per family: counting, user, and temporal, each sampled from a different underlying classification dataset. We vendor generators for both benchmarks and generate our problems from scratch. We eval our finetune at temperature 0.2 (determined best empirically), GPT-5.4 at API default (required for reasoning mode), and base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at temperature 0 (we found temperature 0 and 0.2 to perform similarly). We disable thinking on base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as we found it to improve performance; both modes produce chain-of-thought tokens before boxing an answer. On RULER, our finetune performs worse than GPT-5.4, while remaining above 85%. On OOLONG-synth, our model starts worse than GPT-5.4, then matches its performance when document size exceeds 40K tokens. At this length, native context performance begins to degrade, and a single model can be overwhelmed with the number of items requiring tracking within its context. On the other hand, agents in our harness operate at 8K token budgets, executing small pieces of an overall decomposition strategy, which scales gracefully to arbitrary lengths. Exact scores for Figure 1 are given in Table 1 , and per problem-family results for our model in Table 2 . A quick note on cost: while we do not quantify costs formally, our finetune is cheaper both by running a smaller model and by scaling agents over document length instead of context window. In particular, our computational complexity is O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) in document size n n , compared to Ω ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Omega(n^{2}) for dense attention architectures. Our finetune is also faster than full document comparisons, particularly when the tree reduce decomposition strategy is chosen, which allows for parallel processing. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper we show training on a bare bones agentic harness is sufficient for a small model with small context to perform as well as a frontier model with 1M token context on long-context evals. While we do not claim full generalization of our finetune, we also do not train on our evaluation distributions. The point of this paper is to show the power of agentic training in contrast to harness engineering, excessive native long context, and lossy compaction. As a side effect we also show the power of synthetic oracle SFT data generated by frontier models (Opus 4.8, 5, 5.5, and Fable 5 and 5.1, in this case). The thesis of the last decade of AI development is that specific model capability can be incorporated into fully-general models by training on a wider distribution. The methods of this paper can be incorporated into frontier model development, so such models exhibit improved agentic performance under context pressure, without wasting tokens. This is in contrast to an external harness which must be applied at runtime. To develop our curriculum into a production recipe, the training distribution would need to be widened and a reinforcement learning stage would likely prove fruitful in supercharging agentic capabilities. We leave this as important future work, outside the scope of this paper or a small research project more generally.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools to write all our code, administer experiments, create figures, search and analyze relevant literature, format references, generate synthetic datasets, propose or refine hypotheses/brainstorming, design or provide feedback on research methodology/experiments, clean and reformat data, support qualitative and thematic data analysis, and interpret results. We have not used generative AI tools to draft parts of this research paper, and the following topics are not applicable to this work: help develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks, formulate mathematical claims, provide critical ingredients for proving mathematical claims, assist in the writing of proofs, and assist with translation. We have reviewed our AI-assisted work, for example, by reviewing AI code and conducting manual audits of synthetic data. sections.heading: Appendix A Harness and prompts
sections.text: The full system prompt and tool descriptions are given in Figure 5 . The full-document prompt, used for single shot baselines, is given in Figure 6 . Benchmark text fields are supplied in Table 3 . Harness responses are given in Table 4 . You are a long-document assistant. The document is ⟨ \langle N ⟩ \rangle tokens long; you cannot see it directly. Your own context window is ⟨ \langle B ⟩ \rangle tokens — the conversation (system prompt, user message, your responses, and all tool results) must fit in this budget or the episode ends. ⟨ \langle task context, if the benchmark provides one ⟩ \rangle You have two tools: - ‘read_chunk(start, end)‘: read the document tokens in [start, end). - ‘spawn_subagent(subtask)‘: delegate to a fresh-context copy of yourself (also ⟨ \langle B ⟩ \rangle tokens) with ‘subtask‘ as the user prompt. The same tools and system prompt as above are inherited by the subagent. When you are confident in the final answer, emit it as \boxed{value} and stop. Tool descriptions (function-calling schema) read_chunk: Read a slice of the document and return the decoded text of tokens [start, end). The document has a fixed length (stated in the system prompt). Each call is capped at the chunk limit; for larger ranges, issue multiple reads or delegate to a subagent. start: First token position to read (inclusive). end: Last token position to read (exclusive). spawn_subagent: Spawn a fresh-context copy of yourself to solve ‘subtask‘; returns the child’s \boxed{} answer. subtask: Sub-problem statement (free text) for the child to solve Figure 5: Agent system prompt , shared by the root and every subagent, and the two tool descriptions. ⟨ \langle N ⟩ \rangle is the document length and ⟨ \langle B ⟩ \rangle the per-agent context budget. The root’s user message is the benchmark question (Table 3 ); a subagent’s user message is the subtask string its parent wrote. System ⟨ \langle task context, if the benchmark provides one ⟩ \rangle You are given a complete document followed by a question about it. Read the document carefully and answer the question. Show your reasoning, then emit your final answer as \boxed{value} and stop. User ⟨ \langle full document text ⟩ \rangle ⟨ \langle question ⟩ \rangle Figure 6: Full-document prompt , used for the single-shot baselines: the whole document is placed in one user message, with no tools and no budget prose. For RULER, whose template embeds the document mid-prompt, the document is instead placed back at the template’s {context} position, reproducing RULER’s own prompt. Benchmark System prompt task context Root user message OOLONG-synth OOLONG’s dataset description, verbatim (its intro, the number of items, the label set) OOLONG’s question, verbatim, + “Put your final answer inside \boxed{}.” RULER None (empty) RULER’s task template, verbatim, with {context} replaced by a pointer to the document (below) + “Reply with the answer inside \boxed{}.” Table 3: Benchmark text fields. The task context is placed in the system prompt, so every subagent inherits it without the parent restating it. For RULER, {context} in the template is replaced by: “[The relevant text is in a separate document accessible via the read_chunk tool — see the system prompt for usage.] (Document length: ⟨ \langle N ⟩ \rangle tokens.)” Event Tool result returned to the calling agent (verbatim) spawn_subagent Subagent ends with a boxed answer The content of its last closed \boxed{…} Subagent exceeds its context budget agent overflowed context Subagent stops without a boxed answer agent did not box an answer Tree node cap reached Error: rollout node budget reached. Solve directly. read_chunk Valid range The decoded text of tokens [start, end) , clamped to the document Empty range after clamping Empty range. Non-integer arguments Error: read_chunk requires integer ‘start’ and ‘end’. Table 4: Harness responses. An agent’s budget counts its whole rendered conversation (system prompt, tool schema, user message, its own turns and every tool result); each generation is capped at the remaining room. A subagent that answers returns only its boxed content, so its reads and reasoning never enter the parent’s context.

N N is the number of problems per task. Tree : recursive halving, with each parent merging its two children’s partials (for retrieval, the half that finds the answer wins). Fold : one agent reads a slice and hands the rest of the document and its accumulator to the next. Every agent in each tree is a training example. We upweight root gradient mass 4x and positive narrativeqa leaves 2x, downsampling negative leaves by half. Each task has prompt jitter to train a wider distribution. sections.heading: Appendix C Training details
sections.text: Our training runs used rank 32 LoRA on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, chat renderer qwen3_5_disable_thinking , cross-entropy loss on assistant tokens only. Small batch training of size 8-64 (you pay per token on Tinker, and small batch training is generally better-behaved per token, particularly on LoRAs ( Marek et al., 2025 ; Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; Masters and Luschi, 2018 ; Keskar et al., 2017 ) ). We used pure Adam optimizer, no weight decay, no gradient clipping, ϵ = {\epsilon}= 1e-12, β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , with constant learning rate between 5e-6 and 1e-5, single epoch training.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.02404v1 [cs.LG] 01 Oct 2026 Trained Agentic Context Management Bryce Sandlund Affiliation: https://brycesandlund.com Abstract We study long context language models. Instead of training long context natively, or designing a long context harness, we train a model over the simplest possible harness: a tool to call itself with any specified prompt and a tool to read tokens in a range from the input context. We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a diverse synthetic dataset using this harness. With only 8,000 tokens of context, our small model is as strong as GPT-5.4 with 1M tokens of context on the OOLONG-synth benchmark when document length exceeds 40K tokens 1 1 1 Our code is available at: https://github.com/brycesandlund/infinite-context . . Figure 1: Results on RULER and OOLONG-synth. Our finetune runs in our harness with an 8K token per-agent context limit. GPT-5.4 (medium reasoning) and base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (thinking disabled) receive the full document with the prompt (see Section 4 and Appendix A for more details). Base Qwen and GPT-5.4 are served with 64K and 1M token context limits, respectively. The OOLONG random baseline follows Bertsch et al. (2025, §2.3) . 1 Introduction As language models boast impressive breakthroughs ( Luong and Lockhart, 2025 ; Wei, 2025 ; OpenAI, 2025b ; Lin and Cheng, 2025 ; OpenAI, 2026a ; OpenAI, 2026h ; OpenAI, 2026c ) , increasing focus is placed on their limitations. The most salient resource constraint of a language model is its context length. Models can process and produce tokens within this limit, but the limit is hard. Model producers have identified this constraint and placed great emphasis on extending it as large as possible, with some model builders touting 10M ( Dangel, 2026 ; Meta AI, 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) and even 100M ( Magic, 2024 ) token context lengths (for reference, the length of the first Harry Potter book is about 100,000 tokens, the full U.S. tax code roughly 3M, and the Linux kernel source code about 300M). While native context scaling is appealing as a concrete engineering problem, it is not the only approach to producing a model capable of processing long documents. In 2021, OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-3 to summarize sections of books, and then summarize those summaries, achieving competitive performance with human summaries on a model with a context length of just 2,048 tokens ( Wu et al., 2021 ) . As the field has matured, agentic harnesses have become viable. MemGPT treats context similarly to an operating system, relying on LLM-invoked function calls to push relevant information in and out of the context window to external memory, achieving effectively expanded virtual context ( Packer et al., 2023 ) . More recently, Recursive Language Models introduced a harness that leverages LLMs’ coding prior: the model is repeatedly invoked in a REPL environment over O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) -sized result snippets, achieving stronger performance than base models on retrieval and aggregation tasks both within context limits, but also beyond them ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . While handcrafted prompts and programmatic environments can be effective in solving long context problems without native long context training, it begs an obvious question: if models can, for example, solve all the problems at the International Collegiate Programming Contest 2 2 2 https://icpc.global/ World Finals ( OpenAI, 2025b ) , or more generally, implement requested features in codebases far larger than context limits ( Marten et al., 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026e ; Anthropic, 2026a ) , can they not be trained to manage context effectively, without human-authored harness crutches ? Such model training internalizes decisions external harnesses hardcode, offering the potential to scale much more generally. We answer this question in this paper, affirmatively. We consider the simplest possible agentic context harness, defined below. The purpose of the harness is to enable capability , without fixing choices or instilling a prior . 1.1 Harness Our harness has two tools: 1. read_chunk(start, end) : Read a slice of the document and return the decoded text of tokens [ start , end ). 2. spawn_subagent(subtask) : Spawn a fresh-context copy of yourself to solve subtask ; returns the child’s \boxed{} answer. Unmodified long-context prompts are provided to the model over a document accessed via the above harness. The system prompt is propagated to child agents and includes the above harness definition, a generic instruction, and task-specific background, in accordance with the respective eval 3 3 3 Precise harness environment is given in Appendix A . . Subagents’ user prompt is specified by the calling model. 1.2 Results We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a diverse synthetic dataset using this harness and achieve the following results (see Figure 1 ): 1. On the OOLONG-synth benchmark, with a context limit of just 8K tokens per agent, our small model performs as well as GPT-5.4 with 1M tokens of context when document length exceeds 40K tokens. 2. On the RULER benchmark, with a context limit of just 8K tokens per agent, our model scores ≥ 85 % \geq 85\% on document size from 10K to 320K tokens. 1.3 Paper Organization In the next section, we survey related work to frame the contribution of the following sections. In Section 4 , we discuss our experiments, and we conclude in Section 5 . 2 Related Work Long-context LLM work can be broken into a few distinct categories: native long context models , context compaction , and long context harnesses , both trained and untrained. 2.1 Native Long Context Models GPT-2 shipped with a 1,024 token context limit ( Radford et al., 2019 ) . This limit doubled in every generation through GPT-4 ( Brown et al., 2020 ; OpenAI, 2022 ; OpenAI, 2023a ) , until jumping to the 100K range on GPT-4 Turbo ( OpenAI, 2023b ) , with contemporaneous models Claude 2 ( Anthropic, 2023 ) and later Llama 3.1 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) at similar limits. The core difficulty in scaling context length n n in the classic Transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) is Ω ⁡ ( n 2 ) \Omega(n^{2}) attention complexity, which becomes prohibitively expensive as n ≫ 100 n\gg 100 K. State-space architectures like the mamba lineage ( Gu and Dao, 2024 ; Dao and Gu, 2024 ; Lahoti et al., 2026 ) , neural methods like Titans ( Behrouz et al., 2024 ) , and Linear Transformer ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ) derivatives DeltaNet ( Schlag et al., 2021 ) and Gated DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2025 ) abandon quadratic attention for recurrence. Modern architectures are hybrid, combining linear or sparse attention layers with dense attention, allowing context lengths to scale to 1M+ tokens while retaining long-context performance ( Qwen Team, 2026 ; Kimi Team, 2026b ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; GLM-5 Team, 2026 ; NVIDIA, 2025 ; Gemma Team, 2024 ; Mistral AI, 2024 ) . 2.2 Context Compaction An alternative to native long context, and an inevitability when such native context fills, is a function f f mapping current context x x to a reduced context y y where | y | ≪ | x | |y|\ll|x| . Three categories of such lossy f f exist: masking , summarization , and learned compaction . The simplest compaction technique is masking: dropping tokens based on a predetermined rule. Clearing tool call results is a popular recommended choice ( Anthropic, 2025a ) , achieving results competitive with summarization ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Lindenbauer et al., 2025 ) . Alternative approaches evict tokens based on attention statistics ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Summarization is the current production harness default, implemented in Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI ( Anthropic, 2025a ; OpenAI, 2026b ; Google, 2026 ; Barbaste et al., 2026 ) . Trained compaction is a new frontier, described as part of GPT-5.1-Codex-Max ( OpenAI, 2025a ) and Cursor’s composer ( Cassano and Rush, 2026 ) training. “Still” trains a model to compress KV-Cache directly ( O’Neill et al., 2026 ) . 2.3 Long Context Harnesses As long as LLMs have proven useful, an evolving line of work has focused on how to expand their capabilities without touching model internals. The first efforts were known as prompt engineering ( Phoenix and Taylor, 2024 ; Berryman and Ziegler, 2024 ) , which, though necessary on pre-trained base models ( Brown et al., 2020 ) , became internalized through instruction-tuning and reasoning RL ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Function-calling has led to a new wave of such efforts, where domain-specific knowledge, tools, and multi-agent systems live on a scaffold that interacts with powerful LLMs known as a “harness” ( Lopopolo, 2026 ; Barbaste et al., 2026 ) . Long-context harnesses originate with systems like MemGPT ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , RAPTOR ( Sarthi et al., 2024 ) , and Chain of Agents ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , where the overall goal is to engineer workflows that decompose documents into contexts independent LLM calls can read and aggregate. Recursive Language Models is a popular recent example that allows for controlled-depth recursive LLM calls via a programmatic environment ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Follow-up work expands subagent capabilities ( Lumer et al., 2026 ) , trains shared parent/child policies ( Kim and Ahmad, 2026 ) , and incorporates self-reflection ( Alizadeh et al., 2026 ) . Memagent ( Yu et al., 2026 ) trains a harness that walks linearly through context, using RL and a harness prompt to determine what to carry from node-to-node. Similarly to our work, they also use a small (8K token) context while processing long (as much as 3.5M token) documents. However, they test primarily on the distribution they train, compare only against other small models, and hardcode execution path and prompts in the harness. Frontier models now utilize multi-agent systems. Kimi K2.5 trains “agent swarm” ( Kimi Team, 2026a ) : the model is trained to call subagents via reinforcement learning. Subagent trajectories are not trained. OpenAI has also trained multi-agent behavior ( OpenAI, 2026d ) , notably utilizing 10,000 agents to solve Navier-Stokes ( OpenAI, 2026c ) and disclosing cooperatively trained agents in the HuggingFace incident ( OpenAI, 2026f ; Greenblatt et al., 2026 ) . Anthropic, DeepMind, Meta, and xAI likely do similarly, with multi-agent systems touted in respective model and product releases ( Anthropic, 2025b ; Anthropic, 2026b ; OpenAI, 2026g ; xAI, 2026 ; xAI, 2025 ; Meta Superintelligence Labs, 2026 ; Google, 2025 ; Gottweis et al., 2026 ) . 3 Methods We deliberately use the minimal tool definitions necessary to train agentic context management. However, our harness is sufficient to allow arbitrarily complex multi-agent decompositions. Decompositions in the literature fall into roughly three categories: tree reduce ( Wu et al., 2021 ; Sarthi et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ) , sequential folds ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and agentic delegation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Kimi Team, 2026a ; Anthropic, 2025b ) . We utilize all three strategies. Without any training, models generally make poor use of our harness. Base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.6 use subagent delegation sporadically, sometimes choosing to read the entire document in one context, even if context limit is specified to be less than document length, and other times delegating the exact original question to subagents. Opus 4.6 does slightly better, showing real context pressure awareness and document range subagent delegation. Unfortunately it delegates too much, blowing through $300 of API credits building massive subagent trees on a 100-question eval, only to overcount 4 4 4 Opus 4.6 does appear to perform somewhat decently on our harness with unlimited context budget. Unfortunately, due to the massive subagent trees, running the full comparison without restriction is cost-prohibitive. . Instead, we compare to base models supplied the entire document in context with native context limits, where performance is stronger. In general, models have a weak prior for context decomposition. Pre-training is pure language continuation, and agentic post-training does not teach decomposition strategies. Where Recursive Language Models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) can rely on strong coding priors instilled in both pre- and post-training, decomposition on our harness needs to be taught. One idea might be to RL an open weight model on our harness. Unfortunately, exploration in LLM RL is far too weak to escape the weak decomposition prior at modest compute budgets. It is also unclear what reward to assign subagents, and if GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) or its derivatives ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) are used, what group to compare subagent trajectories in. We instead SFT a decomposition strategy. We train tree reduce for order-independent tasks (see Figure 2 ), sequential fold for order-dependent tasks (see Figure 3 ), and agentic delegation to handle boundary conditions whenever we read the document (see Figure 4 ). By not hardcoding a decomposition structure in our harness, our model internalizes and composes delegation strategies according to the task and current problem-solving state. We generate synthetic oracle demonstration data on a wide distribution of aggregation, retrieval, and sequential tasks. While we cover similar shapes to our evals, our training distribution uses independent questions and vastly more diverse examples. The technical challenge is to instill the necessary prior so the model knows how to take a question and delegate appropriate subtasks to agents from which the final answer can be determined. For example, consider the training question “In how many sections are there STRICTLY more named than unnamed sentences?” (the prompt defines a named sentence as a sentence with a proper noun). To answer this question, each leaf must compute a tally of named and unnamed sentences per section in its assigned range. Thus, the root must recognize the necessary, often multi-dimensional, key space and dictate this and a recursive strategy to mid-level agents, who pass the instruction down to other mid-level agents, until leaves compute their range and counts are aggregated back up the tree, culminating in a final judgement at the root. Our training data is primarily record-based, but also includes real prose, dot-separated word lists, and haystacks with injected needles. We finetune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, chosen as a capable small model with affordable compute, trained on the Tinker platform ( Thinking Machines Lab, 2025a ; Thinking Machines Lab, 2025b ) . For more details on our complete training data and hyperparameters, see Appendices B and C , respectively. We do consider an RL stage following SFT. Unfortunately, even with LLM-as-a-judge rewards on subagent trajectories, as described in Recursive Agent Optimization ( Gandhi et al., 2026 ) , the policy exhibits high-variance and latches onto simpler strategies that weaken overall performance. We suspect RL to be useful in learning recovery and strengthening generalization; however, to do this properly probably requires group-level baselines on subagent trajectories, to cut variance, and compute beyond the scope of this paper. 4 Experiments We test our finetune on RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , the standard long context eval, and OOLONG-synth ( Bertsch et al., 2025 ) , a newer long context benchmark frontier models have not yet saturated, also used in Recursive Language Models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , Recursive Agent Optimization ( Gandhi et al., 2026 ) , and Recursive Agent Harnesses ( Lumer et al., 2026 ) . RULER is an extension of needle-in-a-haystack style tasks with variable tracking, word frequencies, and Q&A. OOLONG-synth concatenates classification tasks on ten datasets into long documents on which aggregation is queried. While we do not eval against additional frontier models, due to compute requirements, we recommend the reader read the OOLONG paper for more comparisons (GPT-5 tops the chart) ( Bertsch et al., 2025 ) . For more RULER reference points, consult model release cards ( NVIDIA, 2025 ; GLM-5 Team, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Dangel, 2026 ) . For RULER, we fix a sample of 5 questions per problem type, for a total of 65 problems per document length. For OOLONG-synth, we fix a sample of 10 questions per family: counting, user, and temporal, each sampled from a different underlying classification dataset. We vendor generators for both benchmarks and generate our problems from scratch. We eval our finetune at temperature 0.2 (determined best empirically), GPT-5.4 at API default (required for reasoning mode), and base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at temperature 0 (we found temperature 0 and 0.2 to perform similarly). We disable thinking on base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as we found it to improve performance; both modes produce chain-of-thought tokens before boxing an answer. On RULER, our finetune performs worse than GPT-5.4, while remaining above 85%. On OOLONG-synth, our model starts worse than GPT-5.4, then matches its performance when document size exceeds 40K tokens. At this length, native context performance begins to degrade, and a single model can be overwhelmed with the number of items requiring tracking within its context. On the other hand, agents in our harness operate at 8K token budgets, executing small pieces of an overall decomposition strategy, which scales gracefully to arbitrary lengths. Distribution mismatch also arises at 160K+ document length (it sees ≤ \leq 14K doc size in training). 5 Conclusion In this paper we show training on a bare bones agentic harness is sufficient for a small model with small context to perform as well as a frontier model with 1M token context on long-context evals. While we do not claim full generalization of our finetune, we also do not train on our evaluation distributions. The point of this paper is to show the power of agentic training in contrast to harness engineering, excessive native long context, and lossy compaction. As a side effect we also show the power of synthetic oracle SFT data generated by frontier models (Opus 4.8, 5, 5.5, and Fable 5 and 5.1, in this case). The thesis of the last decade of AI development is that specific model capability can be incorporated into fully-general models by training on a wider distribution. The methods of this paper can be incorporated into frontier model development, so such models exhibit improved agentic performance under context pressure, without wasting tokens. This is in contrast to an external harness which must be applied at runtime. To develop our curriculum into a production recipe, the training distribution would need to be widened and a reinforcement learning stage would likely prove fruitful in supercharging agentic capabilities. We leave this as important future work, outside the scope of this paper or a small research project more generally.
